docs.text: HardFOC driver DYNAMIXEL Driver ¶ A C++17 driver for ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL X-series smart servos over Protocol 2.0. It pings and identifies servos, sets the operating mode, commands position, velocity and PWM, reads telemetry and runs sync reads and writes, on any MCU with a half-duplex UART. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that writes and reads bytes on a UART and tells the time; it does the rest: Protocol 2.0 packets and CRC (through the official ROBOTIS SDK), reply timeouts, local-echo handling, the X-series control table and error mapping. Smart servo actuators, Protocol 2.0 DYNAMIXEL X-series ROBOTIS Servos XC430-W150 (validated), XC430-W240, XL430-W250, XM430-W210 / W350, XH430-W210 / W350, other X-series by fallback Bus Half-duplex TTL (3-pin) or RS-485 (4-pin) multidrop, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit Speed 9600 bit/s to 4.5 Mbit/s; factory default 57600 bit/s Addressing IDs 0 to 252, factory ID 1; broadcast ID 254 ( 0xFE ) Supply (servo) XC430-W150: 6.5 V to 14.8 V, 12 V recommended; XM430-W350: 10.0 V to 14.8 V Modes the driver uses Position, extended position, velocity, PWM; current is a raw register write XC430-W150 e-Manual · XM430-W350 e-Manual · Protocol 2.0 What you get ¶ A bus and a device. dynamixel::Bus owns one serial line; dynamixel::Device is one servo on it, with typed calls for torque, mode, goals and telemetry. See API guide . Model-aware. Identify() pings the servo and binds its control table from a catalog of seven X-series models, or a shared X-series fallback. See Model support . The official protocol engine. Packets, CRC and sync instructions come from the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK 4.1.0, hidden behind the public headers. See SDK integration . Results you can act on. Every call returns a DriverResult with a DriverError and the raw SDK and device codes; a write whose reply was lost is UncertainOutcome , not a silent failure. See API guide . Any half-duplex wiring. Direction buffer, auto-direction transceiver or single wire with local echo: the transport decides, the driver never touches a pin. See Porting . Safe by construction. No constructor opens the UART, enables torque or moves a servo. See Quickstart . Tested without hardware. Host tests run the real SDK against a scripted transport. See Testing and CI . API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: open the bus, find and identify servos, move them, read them, talk to several at once and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with MyUart the transport from Porting and DriverError standing for dynamixel::DriverError . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ Class Owns Bus One serial line: open, baud rate, ping, scan, register reads and writes by ID, sync read and write Device One servo on a bus: identify, torque, operating mode, motion profile, goals, telemetry ModelDescriptor A servo's control-table addresses and capabilities; the catalog is in dynamixel_model.hpp Transport<Derived> , TransportView Your UART class and the view the bus holds of it Every call is noexcept and returns DriverResult<T> : value , error and detail (the SDK result code, the servo's error byte, byte counts and a timestamp). It converts to bool : if (!servo.ReadPosition()) means it failed. ToString(error) names the error. Open the bus ¶ dynamixel :: TransportConfig cfg {}; cfg . baud_rate = 57600 ; // must match the servo's Baud Rate (address 8) cfg . echo_policy = dynamixel :: EchoPolicy :: None ; // ExpectedLocalEcho on a single-wire link cfg . latency_ms = 2 ; // slack added to every reply timeout const auto opened = bus . Open ( cfg ); if ( ! opened ) { std :: printf ( "open: %s 
 " , dynamixel :: ToString ( opened . error ). data ()); return false ; } Create the bus with braces, dynamixel::Bus bus{dynamixel::TransportView{uart}}; , and keep uart alive as long as the bus. Open() calls your transport's open() ; it sends nothing. Configuration lists every TransportConfig field. Find the servos ¶ uint8_t ids [ 16 ]; const auto found = bus . Scan ( ids , 16 , 0 , 20 ); // ping IDs 0..20, keep up to 16 answers for ( uint8_t i = 0 ; found && i < found . value ; ++ i ) { const auto ping = bus . Ping ( ids [ i ]); if ( ping ) { std :: printf ( "id %u model %u fw %u 
 " , ids [ i ], ping . value . model_number , ping . value . firmware_version ); } } Scan() pings each ID in turn and costs one reply timeout per absent ID, so keep the range short. Any device ID from 0 to 252 is valid (Protocol 2.0, section 2.3); the default range is all of them. ID 253 is not a device ID and 254 is the broadcast ID, so Scan() , Ping() , ReadRegister() and the sync calls reject them. Identify a servo ¶ const auto ping = servo . Identify (); // ping, catalog lookup, read Operating Mode if ( ping . error == DriverError :: UnsupportedRequest ) { // The servo answered; ping.value.model_number is not in kKnownModels. servo . BindXSeriesFallback (); // shared X-series addresses } else if ( ! ping ) { return false ; } std :: printf ( "%s 
 " , servo . model () -> name ); Identify() binds the servo's ModelDescriptor and caches its operating mode. Until a model is bound, the typed calls below return UnsupportedRequest . Model support explains the catalog and the fallback. Move to a position ¶ // Operating Mode is in EEPROM: torque must be off to change it. if ( ! servo . SetTorqueEnabled ( false ) || ! servo . SetOperatingMode ( dynamixel :: OperatingMode :: Position ) || ! servo . SetMotionProfile ( 20 , 50 )) { // Profile Acceleration, Profile Velocity return false ; } const auto here = servo . ReadPosition (); // never command a goal you did not read near if ( ! here || ! servo . SetTorqueEnabled ( true )) { return false ; } return servo . SetGoalPosition ( here . value + 64 ). ok (); // 64 ticks = 5.6 degrees Operating Mode is an EEPROM register: SetOperatingMode() reads Torque Enable first and returns Busy if torque is on. It never turns torque off for you. A goal for a mode the servo is not in returns UnsupportedRequest without sending anything. OperatingMode Goal call Unit (XC430-W150) Position (3, factory): 0 to 360° SetGoalPosition() 1 pulse, 4096 per turn ExtendedPosition (4): multi-turn SetGoalPosition() 1 pulse Velocity (1) SetGoalVelocity() 0.229 rev/min Pwm (16): voltage SetGoalPwm() 0.113 % SetMotionProfile(acceleration, velocity) writes Profile Acceleration (address 108) and Profile Velocity (112), which shape every position move; 0 means unlimited. Spin at a velocity ¶ if ( ! servo . SetTorqueEnabled ( false ) || ! servo . SetOperatingMode ( dynamixel :: OperatingMode :: Velocity ) || ! servo . SetTorqueEnabled ( true )) { return false ; } return servo . SetGoalVelocity ( 44 ). ok (); // 44 x 0.229 rev/min = about 10 rev/min Read state ¶ const auto tel = servo . ReadTelemetry (); if ( ! tel ) { return ; // the position read failed } const auto & t = tel . value ; std :: printf ( "pos %ld vel %ld pwm %d %u.%u V %u C hw 0x%02x 
 " , static_cast < long > ( t . position ), static_cast < long > ( t . velocity ), t . pwm , t . voltage_0p1_v / 10U , t . voltage_0p1_v % 10U , t . temperature_c , t . hardware_error ); if ( servo . model () -> effort_is_current ) { std :: printf ( "current %d x 2.69 mA 
 " , t . load ); // XM / XH: Present Current } else { std :: printf ( "load %d x 0.1 %% 
 " , t . load ); // XC / XL: Present Load } ReadTelemetry() makes two reads: one of the contiguous Present block, Present PWM (124) to Present Temperature (146), 23 bytes, and one of Hardware Error Status (70). It fails when the block read fails; hardware_error stays 0 when its own read fails, and detail is the block read's. When the block reply would not fit max_packet_bytes or the servo refuses the range with an error number, it falls back to one read per register, which fails only when the position read fails. For one value, ReadPosition() is a single read. For several servos at once, use a sync read. Read or write several servos at once ¶ const uint8_t ids [ 2 ] = { 1 , 2 }; uint8_t pos1 [ 4 ] = {}, pos2 [ 4 ] = {}; uint8_t * const out [ 2 ] = { pos1 , pos2 }; dynamixel :: SyncReadItem items [ 2 ]; const auto got = bus . SyncRead ( 132 , 4 , ids , 2 , out , items ); // Present Position, both servos if ( ! got || got . value != 2 ) { return false ; // items[i].valid says which one is missing } const uint8_t goal1 [ 4 ] = { 0x00 , 0x08 , 0 , 0 }; // 2048, little-endian const uint8_t goal2 [ 4 ] = { 0x00 , 0x04 , 0 , 0 }; // 1024 const uint8_t * const in [ 2 ] = { goal1 , goal2 }; return bus . SyncWrite ( 116 , 4 , ids , in , 2 ). ok (); // Goal Position, one packet, no replies A sync write is one broadcast packet and no replies. A sync read is one request and one status packet per servo; SyncRead() collects each reply on its own, so a missing servo marks only its own SyncReadItem invalid and the return value is the number of valid replies. Both take one address and length for all servos, little-endian payloads. Use any register directly ¶ uint8_t delay = 0 ; // Return Delay Time, address 9, 2 us per unit if ( ! servo . ReadRegister ( 9 , & delay , 1 )) { return false ; } const uint8_t shorter = 0 ; // EEPROM: torque must be off return servo . WriteRegister ( 9 , & shorter , 1 , dynamixel :: WritePolicy :: ReadbackVerify ). ok (); ReadRegister() and WriteRegister() work with or without a bound model, on the Device or on the Bus by ID. The write policy says how sure you want to be: WritePolicy Sends Returns success when TxOnly Write, no reply expected The packet left the host (the only policy allowed for the broadcast ID) TxRx (default) Write, waits for the status packet The servo acknowledged it without an error ReadbackVerify Write, then a read of the same bytes The bytes read back match (up to 64 bytes) Change the baud rate ¶ const uint8_t index_1m = 3 ; // Baud Rate (address 8): 3 = 1 Mbit/s const auto wr = servo . WriteRegister ( 8 , & index_1m , 1 ); // EEPROM: torque must be off if ( ! wr ) { return false ; } return bus . SetHostBaudRate ( 1000000 ). ok (); // follow it on the host side Baud Rate (address 8) takes an index, 0 to 7 ( Hardware ). Once the servo runs at the new rate, SetHostBaudRate() moves the host. Every servo on the bus has to follow, or the host loses the ones left behind. Handle errors ¶ const auto r = servo . SetGoalPosition ( 2048 ); switch ( r . error ) { case DriverError :: None : break ; case DriverError :: Timeout : // no status packet: wiring, baud, ID, power case DriverError :: ChecksumError : // corrupted reply: cable, termination, baud std :: printf ( "link: %s 
 " , dynamixel :: ToString ( r . error ). data ()); break ; case DriverError :: UncertainOutcome : // write sent, no reply: it may have applied std :: printf ( "re-read before retrying 
 " ); break ; case DriverError :: DeviceError : // the servo answered with an error byte std :: printf ( "device error 0x%02x 
 " , r . detail . device_error ); break ; default : // UnsupportedRequest: wrong mode or no model std :: printf ( "%s (comm %ld) 
 " , dynamixel :: ToString ( r . error ). data (), static_cast < long > ( r . detail . comm_code )); break ; } DriverError Meaning What to do Timeout No status packet in time Check ID, baud, wiring, power ChecksumError , MalformedResponse A reply arrived, damaged Cable, ground, baud too high for the circuit EchoMismatch Local echo expected and not heard, or wrong Match EchoPolicy to the wiring UncertainOutcome A write was sent and its reply lost Read the register back before retrying DeviceError The servo answered with an error byte detail.device_error : bit 7 hardware alert, bits 0 to 6 the error number UnsupportedRequest No model bound, or wrong mode for the call Identify() or bind a model; change mode Busy Torque on during a mode change, or the bus is mid-transaction Torque off first BufferTooSmall The request's packet is longer than max_packet_bytes ; nothing was sent Split it, or raise the limit ( Configuration ) NotInitialized , InvalidParameter , InvalidId Bus not open, a null buffer or zero length, ID above 252 Fix the call When bit 7 of the error byte is set, read Hardware Error Status (address 70, also in Telemetry::hardware_error ): bit 0 input voltage, bit 2 overheating, bit 3 motor encoder, bit 4 electrical shock, bit 5 overload. On the faults enabled in Shutdown (address 63) the servo clears Torque Enable, and only a reboot turns it back on: a power cycle, or the Reboot instruction. Troubleshooting maps symptoms to causes. Recover from a hardware error ¶ uint8_t hw = 0 ; // Hardware Error Status, address 70 servo . ReadRegister ( 70 , & hw , 1 ); // DeviceError with the Alert bit still fills hw if ( hw == 0 ) { return true ; } std :: printf ( "hardware error 0x%02x, rebooting 
 " , hw ); // fix the cause first (supply, load, heat) const auto rb = servo . Reboot (); // Reboot instruction (0x08) if ( ! rb && rb . error != DriverError :: UncertainOutcome ) { return false ; // UncertainOutcome: it may be rebooting already } for ( int attempt = 0 ; attempt < 20 ; ++ attempt ) { // the servo answers again once it has booted if ( bus . Ping ( servo . id ())) { return true ; // torque is off; RAM is back to its defaults } } return false ; Reboot() (on the Device , or Bus::Reboot(id) ) sends the Reboot instruction, 0x08 (Protocol 2.0, section 5.7). The servo answers before it restarts; the Alert bit in that reply is the fault being cleared, so it does not count as an error, and detail.device_error keeps it. A non-zero error number is DeviceError ; no reply is UncertainOutcome , because the servo may have rebooted anyway. After a reboot the RAM area is back to its defaults: torque is off and Hardware Error Status is 0. The broadcast ID reboots every servo and gets no reply. Fix the cause of the fault first, or it latches again.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches a servo. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Bus per serial line and one Device per servo; the public members listed are the Bus and Device methods from inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp and inc/dynamixel_device.hpp. The bus encodes and decodes Protocol 2.0 packets with the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK, behind a private PortHandler adapter, and reaches the line through TransportView, the type-erased view of a Transport class (inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp). That class is the only code you write: it moves bytes over a half-duplex UART and reads a microsecond clock. Below it are the servos. Drawn from: inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp Bus members ; inc/dynamixel_device.hpp Device members ; inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp Transport hooks ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer Where You change it Core : Bus , Device , model catalog inc/ , src/ Never, for a new board Protocol engine and interface : the SDK, TransportView src/backend/ , inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp Never Platform transport : your class Your project Once per MCU ( Porting ) Everything above the transport is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the test fake. That is how the host tests run the real SDK without a servo. How one call reaches a servo ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as Device participant B as Bus + SDK participant T as Your transport A->>D: SetGoalPosition(2048) D->>D: check model and mode D->>B: WriteRegister(116, 4 bytes) B->>T: discard_stale_input() B->>T: write_some(), finish_transmit() B->>T: read_some() until status or timeout T-->>B: status packet B-->>D: DriverResult D-->>A: DriverResult The SDK's packet handler builds the packet and checks the reply; the private PortHandler adapter translates its clearPort() , writePort() and readPort() calls into the transport calls above. Design choices ¶ The SDK does the protocol. The driver does not reimplement Protocol 2.0: it compiles four SDK source files (packet handler, group handler, sync read, sync write) and gives the SDK a private PortHandler that talks to your transport. Public headers never include the SDK. SDK integration has the details. CRTP transport, type-erased bus. Your transport derives from Transport<Derived> , so hook calls are resolved at compile time. Bus takes a TransportView (a pointer and a table of function pointers) instead of a template parameter, so Bus and Device are ordinary classes compiled once in src/ . Ownership. The transport outlives the bus; the bus outlives its devices. Bus is movable, not copyable. Nothing happens in a constructor. Constructing a Bus or a Device sends nothing. Identify() only reads. Torque, mode, ID and baud changes are always explicit calls. One owner per bus. Bus is not thread-safe: the SDK's is_using_ flag is not a lock. Give each bus one task, or guard every call with one mutex (hf-core's DynamixelHandler takes an RtosMutex ). docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Unreleased ¶ Documentation moved to the HardFOC MkDocs platform: rewritten pages, the code on the site compiled by the host build from tests/docs/ , a layer figure drawn from the headers, the Doxygen reference under api/ . The Jekyll site and its files are gone. README rewritten to the HardFOC README standard. Added ¶ Bus::Reboot(id) and Device::Reboot() : the Protocol 2.0 Reboot instruction (0x08, e-Manual section 5.7), the software way to clear a latched Hardware Error Status. An Alert-only status reply counts as success; no reply is UncertainOutcome . New kStatusAlertBit and kStatusErrorNumberMask (section 3.2). Fixed ¶ The installed CMake package exports the target as hf::dynamixel , as documented; it was hf::hf_dynamixel , so find_package(hf_dynamixel) consumers could not link the documented name. hf::hf_dynamixel stays as a compatibility target. CI builds a consumer of the install. Device::ReadTelemetry() reads Present PWM (124) to Present Temperature (146), contiguous in the X-series RAM control table, in one Read instead of six, then Hardware Error Status (70): two packets instead of seven, same values. It falls back to per-register reads when the block does not fit max_packet_bytes or the servo refuses the range. The returned detail is now the block read's. TransportConfig::max_packet_bytes now bounds packet sizes; before, nothing read it. ReadRegister() , WriteRegister() , SyncRead() and SyncWrite() return BufferTooSmall without sending when the instruction or status packet (10 or 11 bytes plus parameters, e-Manual Protocol 2.0 section 2.4) would be longer. Bus::Open() returns InvalidParameter below kMinPacketBytes (14) and caps the limit at kSdkMaxPacketBytes (1024, the SDK's buffers). New InstructionPacketBytes() and StatusPacketBytes() . Device::SetGoalPwm() runs the same checks as the other goal setters: it needs a model whose descriptor supports PWM Control Mode (Operating Mode 16) as well as a cached mode of PWM, and refuses before sending. Device::Identify() no longer casts an Operating Mode register value without a typed mode (0, 5 or an undefined value; X-series e-Manual section 2.4, Operating Mode (11)) into OperatingMode . It maps it to the new OperatingMode::Unknown , which every typed goal refuses. New OperatingModeFromRaw() , Device::operating_mode() and Device::operating_mode_raw() ; SetOperatingMode(Unknown) returns InvalidParameter . Bus::Scan() accepts ID 0, and its default range now starts at 0: Protocol 2.0 device IDs are 0 to 252 (e-Manual, Protocol 2.0, section 2.3). ReadRegister() returns InvalidId (was InvalidParameter ) for an ID above 252, and SyncRead() / SyncWrite() now reject such IDs with InvalidId . New IsDeviceId() and kMinDeviceId . Breaking changes ¶ With the default max_packet_bytes of 256, a single read above 245 bytes, a write above 244 bytes or a sync write above 242 bytes of IDs and data now returns BufferTooSmall instead of being sent. Raise max_packet_bytes (up to 1024) for longer transfers. Bus::Open() fails for a max_packet_bytes below 14. Bus::ReadRegister() returns InvalidId (was InvalidParameter ) for an ID above 252; SyncRead() and SyncWrite() reject such IDs. Bus::Scan() with default arguments now pings ID 0 too (253 IDs instead of 252). 0.4.0 ¶ X-series catalog (XC430, XL430, XM430, XH430) plus BindModel / BindXSeriesFallback for a later larger servo. ESP32-C6 and ESP32-S3 examples share one source tree: Kconfig pins, sdkconfig.defaults.<target> , CONFIG_TARGET=esp32s3 for the scripts. Added dynamixel_scan_example . Read-only and motion examples stream telemetry / bind fallback. Jekyll + Doxygen GitHub Pages ( _config/ , ci-docs-publish.yml ). hf-core aggregation: HF_CORE_ENABLE_DYNAMIXEL and DynamixelHandler are documented here and implemented in hf-core. 0.3.0 ¶ Pin DynamixelSDK 4.1.0 and wrap Protocol 2.0 through a private PortHandler adapter. Public CRTP transport, Bus/Device API, XC430-W150 descriptor, sync read/write. Host tests drive the real protocol engine through a scripted transport. ESP-IDF UART example adapter (C6 bring-up, S3 compile target).

Configuration ¶ Every setting the driver exposes, its default and where it lives: the transport configuration, the write policy, model descriptors, and the Kconfig options of the ESP32 examples. Transport configuration ¶ Bus::Open() takes a TransportConfig and hands it to your transport's open() . Field Default Meaning baud_rate 57600 ( kDefaultBaud ) Host rate in bit/s; must match the servos' Baud Rate register echo_policy EchoPolicy::None ExpectedLocalEcho when RX hears every TX byte (single-wire link) latency_ms 2 Slack added to every reply timeout, twice, on top of 2 ms and the packet's byte time max_packet_bytes 256 ( kMaxPacketBytes ) Largest packet the bus sends or asks a servo for; see below max_packet_bytes bounds every packet before byte stuffing. Protocol 2.0 (e-Manual section 2.4) makes an instruction packet 10 bytes plus its parameters and a status packet 11 bytes plus its data, so with the default of 256 a ReadRegister() or SyncRead() returns at most 245 bytes per servo, a WriteRegister() writes at most 244, and a SyncWrite() carries at most 242 bytes of ID plus data. A request that would not fit returns BufferTooSmall without sending. Open() refuses a value below 14 ( kMinPacketBytes , a ping reply) with InvalidParameter and caps a value above 1024 ( kSdkMaxPacketBytes , the SDK's packet buffers). For reads, writes and pings of one servo, the reply timeout for n expected bytes is n × byte time + 2 × latency_ms + 2 ms, measured with your transport's now_us() . Raise latency_ms when the transport adds buffering of its own (a USB serial adapter, an RTOS queue); lower it, and the servos' Return Delay Time, for faster polling. A single-wire link at 1 Mbit/s: dynamixel :: TransportConfig single_wire_config () { dynamixel :: TransportConfig cfg {}; cfg . baud_rate = 1000000 ; cfg . echo_policy = dynamixel :: EchoPolicy :: ExpectedLocalEcho ; // RX hears every TX byte first cfg . latency_ms = 1 ; return cfg ; } With ExpectedLocalEcho the driver reads back each transmitted packet and compares it before it waits for the reply; a missing or different echo is EchoMismatch . Write policy ¶ Every WriteRegister() takes a WritePolicy , TxRx by default: TxOnly for fire-and-forget and broadcast, ReadbackVerify for EEPROM values you must be sure of. The API guide compares them. The typed Device setters always use TxRx . A servo of your own ¶ A ModelDescriptor holds a servo's register addresses, widths and capabilities. For an X-series servo the catalog does not list, MakeXSeries() builds one from the shared table: // An X-series servo the catalog does not list yet: same control table, its own model number. inline constexpr dynamixel :: ModelDescriptor kMyXm540 = dynamixel :: MakeXSeries ( 1120 , "XM540-W270" , /*supports_current=*/ true , /*effort_is_current=*/ true ); void bind_my_servo ( dynamixel :: Device & servo ) { servo . BindModel ( kMyXm540 ); // kept by Identify() when the ping reports model 1120 ( void ) servo . Identify (); } MakeXSeries() argument Set it to number The model number from the e-Manual (Model Number, address 0) name Any label; Device::model()->name returns it supports_current true when the model has Goal Current (address 102) effort_is_current true when address 126 is Present Current rather than Present Load A servo with a different control table needs a ModelDescriptor written field by field; see Model support . Compile-time constants ¶ Constant Value Use kBroadcastId 0xFE Broadcast, TxOnly writes kMaxDeviceId 0xFC Highest ID, 252 kDefaultBaud 57600 Factory rate kMaxPacketBytes 256 Default max_packet_bytes kMinPacketBytes 14 Smallest max_packet_bytes Open() accepts kSdkMaxPacketBytes 1024 Cap on max_packet_bytes (SDK buffers) ESP32 example options ¶ idf.py menuconfig , menu HF Dynamixel Example ( Kconfig.projbuild ): Every option is named CONFIG_HF_DYNAMIXEL_ followed by the name in the first column. Option Default Meaning UART_PORT 1 UART number UART_TX_GPIO 4 (C6), 17 (S3) MCU TX UART_RX_GPIO 5 (C6), 18 (S3) MCU RX UART_DIR_GPIO -1 Buffer direction pin; -1: none DIR_ACTIVE_HIGH y DIR high while transmitting BAUD 57600 Bus rate SERVO_ID 1 ID used when the scan finds nothing SCAN_LAST_ID 20 Scan IDs 1 to this EXPECT_LOCAL_ECHO n EchoPolicy::ExpectedLocalEcho BIND_XSERIES_FALLBACK y Fallback for an unlisted model The per-chip defaults are in sdkconfig.defaults.esp32c6 and sdkconfig.defaults.esp32s3 .

docs.text: Examples ¶ Complete ESP32 applications that exercise the driver on an X-series servo, from a read-only session to a small move. They run on an ESP32-C6 (CI's target) or an ESP32-S3, UART1, wired as on the Hardware page; the transport is hf_dynamixel_esp_uart.hpp . CI builds every app below on each pull request. The apps ¶ App What it shows Source CI dynamixel_readonly_example Scan, identify and stream telemetry; never enables torque dynamixel_readonly_example.cpp yes dynamixel_scan_example List every servo with its model number and catalog entry or fallback dynamixel_scan_example.cpp yes dynamixel_motion_example Small unloaded move from the present position, then torque off dynamixel_motion_example.cpp yes Build and flash one (from examples/esp32 , ESP-IDF environment loaded): ./scripts/build_app.sh dynamixel_readonly_example Release ./scripts/flash_app.sh flash_monitor dynamixel_readonly_example Release Source of this table: examples/esp32/app_config.yml . Set up once ¶ git submodule update --init --recursive # the SDK and the HardFOC ESP-IDF build scripts cd examples/esp32 . $IDF_PATH /export.sh # ESP-IDF v5.5 ./scripts/build_app.sh list # every app and build type The scripts read app_config.yml (the same file this page's table comes from) and build each app as its own firmware image. Calling idf.py directly stops with APP_TYPE not defined . For an ESP32-S3, set the target for the scripts: CONFIG_TARGET = esp32s3 ./scripts/build_app.sh dynamixel_readonly_example Debug The log line uart1 tx=17 rx=18 confirms the S3 pins. First session on a servo ¶ Power the servo from its own supply, join the grounds, 57600 bit/s, one servo, short cable. Flash dynamixel_readonly_example . It scans, identifies and streams telemetry; it never enables torque. Leave it running for 1000 reads with no unexplained errors. Only then run dynamixel_motion_example , unloaded. It reads the present position, sets a goal 64 ticks (about 5.6°) from it, enables torque, then disables it again. What to read in an example ¶ You want to Read Bring a bus up and read telemetry safely dynamixel_readonly_example.cpp List every servo with its model and catalog entry dynamixel_scan_example.cpp Make a first move from the present position dynamixel_motion_example.cpp Bind the fallback for an unlisted model IdentifyOrBind() in main/include/hf_dynamixel_example_app.hpp Write an ESP-IDF transport main/include/hf_dynamixel_esp_uart.hpp The example folder's README has the build commands and the wiring notes.

docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and DYNAMIXEL X-series servos, with which bus settings, and the traps of a half-duplex line. All values here come from the ROBOTIS e-Manual pages for the XC430-W150 , the XM430-W350 and Protocol 2.0 . Other X-series models differ in supply range and in some control-table units: check the e-Manual page of your model. Connectors ¶ The bus is multidrop: every servo shares GND, VDD and DATA, and each answers only to its own ID. Pin TTL (3-pin) RS-485 (4-pin) 1 GND GND 2 VDD (servo supply) VDD (servo supply) 3 DATA DATA+ 4 DATA- Housings are JST EHR-03 (TTL) and EHR-04 (RS-485), with SEH-001T-P0.6 crimp terminals. The XC430-W150 is TTL only; the XM430-W350 comes in a TTL and an RS-485 version. Half-duplex wiring ¶ TTL DATA is one wire that carries both directions, so the MCU's TX and RX must take turns. The transport you write handles the turn-around; the driver never touches a pin. Three wirings work: Wiring Turn-around in the transport EchoPolicy Buffer or RS-485 transceiver with a DIR pin DIR on to send, off in finish_transmit() None Auto-direction transceiver None None TX and RX joined, open drain None; RX hears TX and the driver drops it ExpectedLocalEcho ROBOTIS's reference TTL circuit is designed for a 5 V or 5 V tolerant MCU and says to use a level shifter otherwise. On a 3.3 V MCU such as the ESP32, put a buffer or level shifter rated for both levels between the UART and DATA. A transistor TTL adapter is fine for bench reads at 57600 bit/s; qualify a proper buffer before high baud rates or long cables. RS-485 needs a transceiver with DATA+ and DATA- to pins 3 and 4, and a direction pin unless it switches automatically. Bus settings ¶ Setting Value Format 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, asynchronous Speed 9600, 57600, 115200 bit/s, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 4.5 Mbit/s (Baud Rate, address 8, index 0 to 7) Factory setting 57600 bit/s (index 1), ID 1 IDs 0 to 252; 254 ( 0xFE ) is broadcast Reply delay Return Delay Time (address 9), 2 µs per unit; factory value 250 (500 µs) The host and every servo on the bus must use the same rate. Change a servo's rate with a register write, then follow it with Bus::SetHostBaudRate() ( API guide ). Protocol 2.0 ¶ The host sends an instruction packet and, unless it was broadcast, the addressed servo answers with a status packet. Every multi-byte field is little-endian. Field Instruction packet Status packet Header, reserved FF FF FD 00 FF FF FD 00 ID Target servo, or FE Answering servo Length (2 bytes) Parameters + 3 Parameters + 4 Instruction Ping 01 , Read 02 , Write 03 , Sync Read 82 , Sync Write 83 55 Error Bit 7: hardware alert; bits 0 to 6: error number Parameters, CRC-16 Address and data Data sequenceDiagram participant H as Host (driver) participant S as Servo ID 1 H->>S: Read, address 132, 4 bytes Note over H: finish_transmit(), release the line Note over S: Return Delay Time (500 µs factory) S-->>H: Status, error 0, 4 data bytes The same exchange on the wire, reading Present Position: host -> FF FF FD 00 01 07 00 02 84 00 04 00 CRC_L CRC_H servo -> FF FF FD 00 01 08 00 55 00 p0 p1 p2 p3 CRC_L CRC_H header ID length inst err/params The SDK builds and checks these packets; the driver turns a missing or corrupt status into Timeout or ChecksumError and the error byte into DeviceError . Feed pin 2 from a supply sized for the stall current of every servo on the bus (1.4 A for one XC430-W150 at 12 V), join its ground to the MCU's and keep the logic path between them level-compatible. Present Input Voltage (address 144, 0.1 V per unit) reads the supply at each servo. Control table used by the driver ¶ The driver's X-series descriptor ( inc/dynamixel_model.hpp ) uses these addresses. EEPROM entries can only be written while torque is off. On XM and XH models address 126 is Present Current, 2.69 mA per unit on the XM430-W350. docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a static C++17 library that compiles the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK sources it needs; nothing else. Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler. CI builds with GCC on Ubuntu and with the ESP-IDF v5.5 toolchains (ESP32-C6). CMake 3.16 or newer. A heap: the bus allocates its state once at construction, and the SDK allocates packet buffers on every call ( SDK integration ). No RTOS and no exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns a DriverResult . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose. The driver has its own submodule, the SDK: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-dynamixel-driver.git external/hf-dynamixel-driver git submodule update --init --recursive external/hf-dynamixel-driver Submodule Source Needed for external/DynamixelSDK ROBOTIS-GIT/DynamixelSDK, tag 4.1.0 Every build examples/esp32/scripts hardfoc/hf-espidf-project-tools The ESP32 examples only CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-dynamixel-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::dynamixel ) The hf::dynamixel target ( hf_dynamixel ) carries the include directories, the generated version header and cxx_std_17 . The SDK headers stay private: your code never includes them. Option Default Effect HF_DYNAMIXEL_ENABLE_WARNINGS ON -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic HF_DYNAMIXEL_BUILD_TESTS OFF Host tests, doc snippets ( Testing ) HF_DYNAMIXEL_BUILD_HOST_EXAMPLE OFF examples/host/ping_read.cpp HF_DYNAMIXEL_ENABLE_SANITIZERS ON ASan and UBSan on the host tests Link one copy of the SDK per firmware image. Do not also link a separate upstream dynamixel_sdk target. cmake --install exports the same target as hf::dynamixel ( lib/cmake/hf_dynamixel ) with the public headers; a consumer calls find_package(hf_dynamixel REQUIRED) and links hf::dynamixel . ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is components/hf_dynamixel/CMakeLists.txt (the examples use the copy in examples/esp32/components/hf_dynamixel/ ). Point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it, or copy it into your project's components/ , and set the HF_DYNAMIXEL_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout. It requires the driver and esp_timer components. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_dynamixel . The SDK sources only include their headers when __linux__ , __APPLE__ , WIN32 or ARDUINO is defined, so the build settings define __linux__ for the library's own sources on any toolchain other than Linux, macOS or Windows. The define is private: your code never sees it ( SDK integration ). Inside hf-core ¶ hf-core can compile the driver with its DynamixelHandler and a transport over BaseUart . Turn on HF_CORE_ENABLE_DYNAMIXEL (off by default); the handler and its documentation live in hf-core under handlers/dynamixel/ and docs/handlers/dynamixel_handler.md . How the build is organised ¶ File Role cmake/hf_dynamixel_build_settings.cmake Sources, include directories, version, SDK pin: the single source of truth cmake/hf_dynamixel_sdk_sources.cmake The SDK translation units compiled and their defines CMakeLists.txt Static library, options, install and export The version and the SDK pin are set once in the settings file and written into dynamixel_version.h at configure time. Read them at run time: const char * v = dynamixel :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.4.0" const char * sdk = dynamixel :: GetSdkTag (); // "4.1.0"; GetSdkCommit() gives the hash Next ¶ Quickstart wires a servo and reads it; Porting writes the transport for your MCU.

docs.text: Model support ¶ Which servos the driver knows by model number, what "knows" gives you, and how to run a servo it does not list. The catalog ¶ Device::Identify() pings the servo and looks its model number up in kKnownModels ( inc/dynamixel_model.hpp ). Every entry is built by MakeXSeries() and shares the X-series control table ( Hardware ); they differ only in two flags. Constant Model number Address 126 is kXc430W150 1070 Present Load kXc430W240 1080 Present Load kXl430W250 1060 Present Load kXm430W210 1030 Present Current kXm430W350 1020 Present Current kXh430W210 1010 Present Current kXh430W350 1000 Present Current kXSeriesFallback 0 (any) treated as Present Load The XC430-W150 is the servo the driver was validated on. The XM and XH entries set supports_current and effort_is_current ; read servo.model()->effort_is_current before treating Telemetry::load as current. What a bound model gives you ¶ Without a model, Device 's typed calls return UnsupportedRequest ; ReadRegister() and WriteRegister() still work. With one: Call Needs SetTorqueEnabled() , SetMotionProfile() , ReadPosition() , ReadTelemetry() A model SetOperatingMode() A model, and torque off (else Busy ) SetGoalPosition() Mode Position or Extended Position SetGoalVelocity() Mode Velocity SetGoalPwm() Mode PWM (16), and a model with supports_pwm Identify() also reads the servo's Operating Mode and caches it; SetOperatingMode() updates the cache, and operating_mode() returns it. A register value without a typed mode (current 0, current-based position 5, or a value the control table does not define) is cached as OperatingMode::Unknown , with the raw byte in operating_mode_raw() . A goal for another mode, or any goal while the mode is Unknown , is refused before anything is sent. A servo the catalog does not list ¶ Identify() returns UnsupportedRequest with ping.value.model_number filled in: the servo answered. Call BindXSeriesFallback() to use the shared X-series addresses, or bind a descriptor of your own with BindModel() before calling Identify() again. A bound descriptor survives Identify() when its model_number is 0 or matches the ping. When the part is settled, add a MakeXSeries() entry to kKnownModels , with supports_current and effort_is_current from the model's e-Manual page, so Identify() binds it by itself. Configuration shows a descriptor for the XM540-W270 (model 1120). Out of scope ¶ Protocol 1.0, the MX, AX and DYNAMIXEL-P series: their control tables differ. Typed current control: write Goal Current (address 102) with WriteRegister() and set Operating Mode 0 or 5 yourself. OperatingMode lists only velocity (1), position (3), extended position (4) and PWM (16). Bulk Read and Bulk Write instructions.

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: a UART transport derived from dynamixel::Transport<Self> . The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls eight methods on your class, declared in inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp . The base class uses CRTP, so the calls are resolved at compile time; the bus holds the class through a TransportView , a pointer and a table of function pointers, so Bus itself is not a template. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Bus per serial line and one Device per servo; the public members listed are the Bus and Device methods from inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp and inc/dynamixel_device.hpp. The bus encodes and decodes Protocol 2.0 packets with the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK, behind a private PortHandler adapter, and reaches the line through TransportView, the type-erased view of a Transport class (inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp). That class is the only code you write: it moves bytes over a half-duplex UART and reads a microsecond clock. Below it are the servos. Drawn from: inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp Bus members ; inc/dynamixel_device.hpp Device members ; inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp Transport hooks ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ Method Contract open(cfg) Configure the UART for cfg.baud_rate , 8N1. Send nothing. Return DriverError::None or SerialError close() Release the UART set_baud_rate(baud) Change the host rate only write_some(data, n) Queue up to n bytes; return how many were accepted. A partial write is fine: the driver calls again finish_transmit() Block until the last stop bit is on the wire, then release the line for the reply read_some(out, max) Copy the bytes that have arrived, up to max , without blocking. 0 bytes is not an error discard_stale_input() Drop everything in the receive buffer; called at the start of a transaction now_us() A monotonic microsecond clock; reply timeouts are measured with it delay_ms_impl(ms) , yield_impl() Optional. Without them the base versions do nothing Return DriverError::SerialError (or {0, SerialError} ) only for a UART failure. Timeouts, checksums and echo checks are the driver's job. The transport ¶ my_uart.hpp class MyUart : public dynamixel :: Transport < MyUart > { public : // Configure the UART: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit at cfg.baud_rate. No servo traffic. dynamixel :: DriverError open ( const dynamixel :: TransportConfig & cfg ) noexcept { platform_dir_set ( false ); // listen return platform_uart_set_baud ( cfg . baud_rate ) ? dynamixel :: DriverError :: None : dynamixel :: DriverError :: SerialError ; } void close () noexcept {} dynamixel :: DriverError set_baud_rate ( uint32_t baud ) noexcept { return platform_uart_set_baud ( baud ) ? dynamixel :: DriverError :: None : dynamixel :: DriverError :: SerialError ; } // Queue bytes for transmission; report how many were accepted (a partial write is fine). dynamixel :: TransportIo write_some ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t length ) noexcept { platform_dir_set ( true ); // drive the bus const int n = platform_uart_write ( data , length ); if ( n < 0 ) { return { 0 , dynamixel :: DriverError :: SerialError }; } return { static_cast < std :: size_t > ( n ), dynamixel :: DriverError :: None }; } // Block until the last stop bit has left the pin, then release the bus for the reply. dynamixel :: DriverError finish_transmit () noexcept { const bool done = platform_uart_wait_tx_done (); platform_dir_set ( false ); return done ? dynamixel :: DriverError :: None : dynamixel :: DriverError :: SerialError ; } // Return what has arrived so far; 0 bytes is not an error. dynamixel :: TransportIo read_some ( uint8_t * out , std :: size_t max ) noexcept { const int n = platform_uart_read ( out , max ); if ( n < 0 ) { return { 0 , dynamixel :: DriverError :: SerialError }; } return { static_cast < std :: size_t > ( n ), dynamixel :: DriverError :: None }; } void discard_stale_input () noexcept { platform_uart_flush_rx (); } uint64_t now_us () noexcept { return platform_micros (); } // Optional: lets the driver sleep instead of spinning while it waits. void delay_ms_impl ( uint32_t ms ) noexcept { platform_delay_ms ( ms ); } }; Then bind it, with braces: MyUart uart ; dynamixel :: Bus bus { dynamixel :: TransportView { uart }}; Rules for the half-duplex line ¶ Turn around in finish_transmit() . It must not return before the UART's shift register is empty: release the direction pin earlier and the last byte is cut; later and the start of the reply is lost. The factory Return Delay Time gives you 500 µs. Flip DIR in the transport, nowhere else. Device and Bus never see a pin. With an auto-direction transceiver there is nothing to flip. Single wire, TX and RX joined: leave RX enabled while you transmit and set EchoPolicy::ExpectedLocalEcho . The driver reads back and checks the echo itself; read_some() returns the echo bytes like any others. No delays of your own. The reply timeout already allows for the packet time and latency_ms . docs.text: Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: a UART transport derived from dynamixel::Transport<Self> . The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls eight methods on your class, declared in inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp . The base class uses CRTP, so the calls are resolved at compile time; the bus holds the class through a TransportView , a pointer and a table of function pointers, so Bus itself is not a template. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Bus per serial line and one Device per servo; the public members listed are the Bus and Device methods from inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp and inc/dynamixel_device.hpp. The bus encodes and decodes Protocol 2.0 packets with the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK, behind a private PortHandler adapter, and reaches the line through TransportView, the type-erased view of a Transport class (inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp). That class is the only code you write: it moves bytes over a half-duplex UART and reads a microsecond clock. Below it are the servos. Open ( cfg )) { return -1 ; // your transport's open() failed } dynamixel :: Device servo ( bus , 1 ); // 2. factory ID is 1 const auto ping = servo . Identify (); // ping + catalog lookup if ( ping . error == dynamixel :: DriverError :: UnsupportedRequest ) { servo . BindXSeriesFallback (); // answered, model not in the catalog } else if ( ! ping ) { return -2 ; // Timeout: wiring, power, baud, ID } const auto tel = servo . ReadTelemetry (); // 3. torque stays off if ( ! tel ) { return -3 ; } std :: printf ( "position %ld ticks, %u.%u V \n " , static_cast < long > ( tel . value . position ), tel . value . voltage_0p1_v / 10U , tel . value . voltage_0p1_v % 10U ); return 0 ; } What each step does: Bus::Open() calls your transport's open() with the configuration. docs.text: SDK integration ¶ How the driver uses the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK, which version, and the SDK behaviour you inherit. The pinned SDK ¶ Item Value Repository ROBOTIS-GIT/DynamixelSDK , submodule external/DynamixelSDK Tag 4.1.0 Commit f838bc90f72fcf5b9c279432d6e12fc24969daa8 Licence Apache-2.0 ( THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES ); the driver is MIT dynamixel::GetSdkTag() and GetSdkCommit() return the pin the binary was built with. What the driver takes from the SDK ¶ Protocol2PacketHandler::getInstance() , the SDK's singleton, for every packet. GroupSyncWrite for Bus::SyncWrite() . Four source files, listed in cmake/hf_dynamixel_sdk_sources.cmake : protocol2_packet_handler.cpp , group_handler.cpp , group_sync_read.cpp , group_sync_write.cpp . None of the SDK's Linux, Windows or Arduino port handlers is compiled. The SDK talks to a PortHandler . The driver's private PortHandlerAdapter implements it over your transport: writePort() loops on write_some() , then calls finish_transmit() and checks the echo; readPort() calls read_some() ; the packet timeout is measured with now_us() . It never calls the SDK's getPortHandler() factory. MapCommCode() turns the SDK's result codes into DriverError : SDK code DriverError COMM_SUCCESS None COMM_PORT_BUSY Busy COMM_TX_FAIL , COMM_RX_FAIL SerialError COMM_TX_ERROR InvalidParameter COMM_RX_TIMEOUT Timeout (a write with a reply: UncertainOutcome ) COMM_RX_CORRUPT ChecksumError COMM_NOT_AVAILABLE UnsupportedRequest anything else MalformedResponse The raw code is kept in DriverResult::detail.comm_code . Behaviour you inherit ¶ SDK behaviour Consequence Packet buffers are allocated with malloc on each call The target needs a heap; the driver does not patch it out is_using_ is a flag, not a mutex Bus is not thread-safe; one owner, or a mutex around every call clearPort() before each transmission Stale input is dropped at the start of a transaction only GroupSyncRead fails the whole group when one servo is missing Bus::SyncRead() sends with syncReadTx() and reads each reply with readRx() , so one silent servo leaves the others valid Building the SDK sources on an MCU ¶ The SDK's source files include their headers only when __linux__ , __APPLE__ , WIN32 or ARDUINO is defined. On any other toolchain (ESP-IDF on Xtensa or RISC-V, bare-metal GCC) the build settings add __linux__ as a private define of the driver library. It never reaches your code.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up a DYNAMIXEL bus, their causes and the fix for each. Start with the DriverError and detail of the failing call: detail.comm_code is the SDK's result, detail.device_error the servo's error byte. Timeout is a link problem; DeviceError means the servo heard you. Every ping times out ¶ Cause Fix Baud rate differs from the servo's Try 57600 (factory), then the other seven rates; or scan with ROBOTIS's DYNAMIXEL Wizard Wrong ID Factory ID is 1; Scan() IDs 0 to 20 TX and RX swapped, or wired for the wrong board ESP32-C6 uses GPIO4 / GPIO5, ESP32-S3 GPIO17 / GPIO18 Direction pin stuck in transmit Release it in finish_transmit() ; leave the DIR GPIO at -1 for an auto-direction transceiver No common ground, or servo unpowered Join the grounds; the servo needs its own supply (6.5 V to 14.8 V for an XC430-W150) 3.3 V MCU straight on a 5 V TTL line Use a buffer or level shifter ( Hardware ) EchoMismatch ¶ The transport heard its own transmission when it should not have, or did not hear it when it should. Set EchoPolicy::ExpectedLocalEcho exactly when TX and RX are joined on one wire ( CONFIG_HF_DYNAMIXEL_EXPECT_LOCAL_ECHO in the examples). Replies are sometimes corrupt ¶ ChecksumError or MalformedResponse now and then: the cable is too long or too noisy for the rate, the circuit is too slow for it, or finish_transmit() releases the line too early and clips the last byte. Drop to 57600 to confirm, then fix the circuit before raising the rate again. Identify() returns UnsupportedRequest ¶ The ping worked and the model number is not in the catalog. ping.value.model_number has it. Bind BindXSeriesFallback() for an X-series servo, or a descriptor of your own ( Model support ). A goal call returns UnsupportedRequest ¶ The servo is in another operating mode ( SetGoalVelocity() in Position mode, for example), or no model is bound. Change the mode with torque off, or call Identify() first. A servo left in current mode (0) or current-based position mode (5) by another tool refuses every typed goal: operating_mode() is Unknown and operating_mode_raw() has the register value. Set a supported mode first. SetOperatingMode() returns Busy ¶ Torque is on. Call SetTorqueEnabled(false) first; the driver will not do it for you. A write returns UncertainOutcome ¶ The write went out and no status packet came back. The servo may have applied it. Read the register back before you retry; for an EEPROM change of ID or baud rate, the servo may now answer at the new value. Torque turns itself off ¶ The servo hit a fault enabled in Shutdown (address 63): input voltage, overheating, encoder, electrical shock or overload. Telemetry::hardware_error has the bits ( API guide ). Fix the cause, then call Reboot() or power-cycle the servo: only a reboot clears the fault and lets torque back on ( Recover from a hardware error ). The motion example jumps ¶ dynamixel_motion_example moves 64 ticks from the present position. A dash towards 0 or 2048 means the position read failed and a raw goal was written anyway. Go back to the read-only example until reads are clean. The examples do not configure ¶ APP_TYPE not defined means CMake or idf.py ran without the scripts. Build from examples/esp32 with ./scripts/build_app.sh <app> Debug ; if scripts/ is empty, run git submodule update --init --recursive . An S3 build that still uses C6 pins was started without CONFIG_TARGET=esp32s3 .

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Three layers, one of them yours ¶ Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Bus per serial line and one Device per servo; the public members listed are the Bus and Device methods from inc/dynamixel_bus.hpp and inc/dynamixel_device.hpp. The bus encodes and decodes Protocol 2.0 packets with the ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL SDK, behind a private PortHandler adapter, and reaches the line through TransportView, the type-erased view of a Transport class (inc/dynamixel_transport.hpp). That class is the only code you write: it moves bytes over a half-duplex UART and reads a microsecond clock. Below it are the servos.
